title: You’re Trying So Hard to Give Your Children Everything You Never Had That You May Be Forgetting What They Actually Need
paragraphs: You’re Trying So Hard to Give Your Children Everything You Never Had That You May Be Forgetting What They Actually Need

Sometimes the childhood you survived becomes the blueprint you spend adulthood trying to erase—and without realizing it, you can give your children everything your younger self wanted while overlooking what their souls need most.
Maybe nobody bought you the shoes everyone else had.
Maybe birthdays were quiet because there simply wasn’t enough money.
Maybe you learned not to ask because you already knew the answer.
Maybe you watched other children open presents while pretending you weren’t jealous.
Maybe your classmates went places your family could never afford.
Maybe you remember looking inside the refrigerator and knowing there wasn’t much there.
Or perhaps your deprivation wasn’t financial at all.
Maybe there was food on the table...
but nobody asked how you were doing.
Maybe you had clothes...
but very little affection.
Maybe you had a roof...
but never felt safe underneath it.
Maybe your father provided financially but was emotionally absent.
Maybe your mother was physically there but carrying wounds so deep that tenderness rarely reached you.
Maybe discipline came without affection.
Maybe affection came without stability.
Maybe you learned to become independent before a child should ever have needed to be.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps you made yourself a promise.
My children will never feel what I felt.
You may never have said it aloud.
But you have been keeping that promise for years.
So you work.
And work.
And work.
You buy the better shoes.
The better phone.
The birthday cake you never received.
The toys you once stared at through store windows.
The vacations you could only imagine.
You make sure there is food in the refrigerator because you remember what an almost-empty refrigerator felt like.
You say yes because you remember hearing no.
You rescue them because nobody rescued you.
You soften consequences because yours were sometimes cruel.
You give because you remember going without.
And there is something profoundly understandable about that.
A parent who suffered deprivation naturally wants to spare a child from the same pain.
But there is a question loving parents sometimes need the courage to ask:
Am I raising my child according to what my child truly needs—or according to what my wounded younger self still wishes someone had given me?
Because those are not always the same thing.
You can give your children everything you never had...
and accidentally fail to give them what God says matters most.
Moses spoke words thousands of years ago that cut straight through the noise of modern parenting.
Deuteronomy 6:6–7 reads in Hebrew:
וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם עַל־לְבָבֶךָ׃ וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ וְדִבַּרְתָּ בָּם בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ וּבְשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ׃
The sense is beautifully direct:
These words God commands are first to be upon your own heart, and then you are to impress them upon your children—speaking of them at home, along the way, when lying down, and when rising.
Notice the order.
Before God's truth reaches the child...
it is supposed to live in the parent.
Before instruction comes discipleship.
Before teaching comes embodiment.
Before your child hears what you believe, your child watches how you live.
And there is something especially powerful in the Hebrew verb translated “teach diligently” or “impress”: וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם — veshinnantam.
It carries the idea of impressing or inculcating these words upon your children. The underlying verb is associated with sharpening.
That gives the command an unforgettable texture.
God's truth is not supposed to be an occasional religious decoration hanging somewhere around the edges of family life.
It is to be repeatedly impressed upon the next generation.
At home.
On the road.
At bedtime.
In the morning.
In other words...
ordinary life becomes the classroom.
Your kitchen can become a classroom.
The drive to school can become a classroom.
The moment after your child fails can become a classroom.
The argument at the dinner table can become a classroom.
The moment your child catches you doing something wrong can become one of the greatest classrooms of all—if instead of defending yourself, you humble yourself and say:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Imagine what that teaches.
Your child discovers that Christianity is not pretending Christians never fail.
Christianity is knowing where sinners go when they do.
To Jesus.
This is where parenting becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the greatest inheritance you can leave your children is not a childhood containing everything you lacked.
It is a home in which they repeatedly encounter what every human being desperately needs.
Truth.
Love.
Boundaries.
Presence.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
And Jesus Christ at the center of it all.
Your children need food.
Provide it.
They need clothing.
Provide it.
They need education and opportunities.
Give what you responsibly can.
There is nothing inherently wrong with birthdays, toys, technology, vacations, comfortable homes, beautiful memories, or financial provision.
But never confuse giving your children more with necessarily giving them better.
A child can live in a beautiful bedroom and feel profoundly alone.
A teenager can hold the newest phone while desperately wishing Dad would put his own phone down and listen.
A child can have shelves filled with toys and still wonder whether Mom enjoys being around them.
A family can take expensive vacations and still be emotionally disconnected.
And a child can know every Christian song while having almost no idea what repentance, grace, forgiveness, holiness, or the cross actually means because those realities were rarely lived before them.
Sometimes what children desperately need cannot be purchased.
They need your eyes when they speak.
They need appropriate affection.
They need boundaries strong enough to make them feel secure.
They need correction that does not humiliate them.
They need consequences that teach rather than merely punish.
They need to know that “no” can sometimes be an expression of love.
They need to watch you forgive.
They need to watch you apologize.
They need to hear you pray when life hurts.
They need to see you open Scripture when nobody is watching.
They need to discover that Jesus is not merely Someone your family talks about on Sunday.
He is Lord on Monday morning.
Lord when money is tight.
Lord when Dad is angry.
Lord when Mom is exhausted.
Lord when somebody fails.
Lord when the diagnosis comes.
Lord when prayers seem unanswered.
Lord when nobody understands.
Lord when the family is celebrating.
Lord when the family is breaking.
Lord when there is plenty.
Lord when there is little.
Because one day your children will leave your house.
The toys will disappear.
The shoes will be outgrown.
The phones will become obsolete.
The clothes will be donated.
The bedrooms may belong to someone else.
The photographs will remain, but childhood itself will be gone.
And your children will enter a world that will not always protect them.
Their hearts may be broken.
They may experience rejection.
They may lose jobs.
Friends may betray them.
People they love will eventually die.
They may encounter temptations you cannot intercept.
They may make decisions you cannot control.
There will come a night when they are hurting somewhere you cannot reach them.
And on that night, the most important thing you gave them will not be sitting inside a bank account.
It will be what was planted inside their souls.
Do they know where to run when shame whispers, Hide?
Do they know there is grace at the feet of Jesus?
Do they know that sin destroys, but Christ receives repentant sinners?
Do they know that failure does not have to become their identity?
Do they know how to pray when Mom and Dad are not there to pray for them?
Do they know the Scriptures because they watched you treasure them?
Do they know that repentance is not humiliation but a turning homeward toward God?
Do they know the Gospel?
Not merely Christianity as culture.
Not merely church attendance.
Not merely Christian merchandise, Christian vocabulary, or Christian social media.
The Gospel.
That all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
That sin is not merely the bad behavior of other people but rebellion residing in every human heart.
That we cannot purchase, perform, inherit, or behave our way into reconciliation with a holy God.
That Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came for sinners.
That He died for sins.
That He rose again.
That forgiveness is offered through Him.
That we are called to repent and believe.
That grace does not merely excuse us—it begins transforming us.
That Jesus does not merely improve our old story.
He gives sinners a new one.
And maybe this is where your own story needs to meet His again.
Because perhaps you have been parenting from an old wound.
You weren't trying to spoil your children.
You were trying to protect them.
You weren't trying to replace love with possessions.
You were trying to make sure they never stared through the same windows you once stared through.
You weren't trying to become absent.
You were working all those hours because you remembered what poverty felt like.
You weren't trying to avoid discipline.
You simply remembered how discipline felt when anger and fear were attached to it.
You were trying to break a cycle.
But sometimes, in our determination to run away from one ditch, we run directly into another.
The answer is not shame.
The answer is surrender.
Bring the wounded child inside you to Christ.
You do not have to make your children responsible for healing the childhood you never had.
You do not need to recreate your childhood through them and then repair it by giving them everything you wanted.
Jesus can meet you there.
He can touch memories your children were never created to heal.
He can expose patterns without discarding you.
He can convict without crushing you.
He can teach you another way.
And perhaps tonight, instead of buying something else, you sit beside your child.
Ask a question.
Then actually listen.
Perhaps you tell them something you have never said enough:
“I love you.”
Perhaps you admit:
“I know I work a lot because I want to give you a better life. But I never want the things I give you to replace the time I should give you.”
Maybe your child is older now.
Maybe years have already passed.
Maybe reading this hurts because you see things you wish you had done differently.
Then remember the Gospel you are supposed to teach them.
Grace is for parents too.
Repentance means you do not have to pretend yesterday was right in order to begin walking differently today.
Perhaps one of the greatest spiritual lessons your grown son or daughter could ever receive is watching a parent become humble enough to say:
“I see things now that I didn't see then. I was trying to love you the best way I knew how, but sometimes my own wounds shaped the way I parented you. Where I failed you, please forgive me.”
That is not weakness.
That is discipleship in flesh and blood.
Your children do not need a flawless Christian parent.
They need to see what a Christian does with failure.
We confess.
We repent.
We seek forgiveness.
We receive grace.
We get back up.
We follow Jesus again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the scandal in your story was poverty.
Maybe abandonment.
Maybe addiction lived in your childhood home.
Maybe abuse.
Maybe emotional neglect.
Maybe divorce.
Maybe nobody taught you how healthy families communicate.
Maybe nobody prayed over you.
Maybe nobody tucked you into bed and told you that you were loved.
Maybe you are building a family without ever having seen a healthy one up close.
Then hear this carefully:
Your past can explain some of your patterns without becoming the master of your future.
Jesus Christ can interrupt what generations repeated.
The cycle does not have to continue merely because it reached you.
But breaking generational patterns requires more than giving children the opposite childhood.
It requires giving Christ access to the parent.
Because Deuteronomy does not begin:
“Put these words on your children's hearts.”
It begins with God's words upon yours.
Then teach them.
Then talk about them.
Then live them in the rhythms of ordinary life.
Your children are not merely listening to your theology.
They are studying your reactions.
They are learning what Christianity looks like when somebody irritates you.
When bills arrive.
When you are exhausted.
When somebody insults you.
When you are wrong.
When nobody is applauding.
When temptation comes.
When suffering comes.
And someday they may forget many of the things you bought them.
But they may remember seeing you on your knees.
They may remember hearing their name in your prayers.
They may remember the night you apologized.
They may remember that when everything went wrong, their mother still whispered, “Jesus, help us.”
They may remember their father opening a Bible at a kitchen table.
They may remember correction followed by an embrace.
They may remember that truth mattered in your house—but grace lived there too.
And perhaps years from now, when their own life begins falling apart, that memory will return.
Not the expensive shoes.
Not the newest phone.
Not the vacation.
Your faith.
Your presence.
Your repentance.
Your prayers.
Your Jesus.
That is why this message is worth sharing.

Some parent on your Facebook feed may be exhausting themselves trying to give their children everything they never had, and nobody has ever gently told them that their child may need them more than another thing.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Send it privately to the parent carrying childhood wounds nobody else sees.
Because parenting has a way of making us forget what matters when life becomes loud.
And if God has already begun changing the way you love your children, tell your testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that families can change.
But let us keep the language biblical.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
The sense is that each should give according to what has been purposed in the heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.

So if you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, do it first by belonging wholly to Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, serving faithfully, giving generously where He leads you, and making the Gospel known.
And whether or not you are able to support financially, you can still help carry the message.
Save the messages you need to return to.
Because perhaps the greatest thing you can leave your children is not proof that you could afford to give them everything.
Perhaps it is the memory that when you finally understood what mattered most...
you gave them yourself.
You gave them truth.
You gave them discipline wrapped in love.
You gave them repentance without hypocrisy.
You gave them forgiveness.
You gave them the example of a life continually returning to the cross.
And above everything else, you kept pointing beyond yourself...
to Jesus.
One day your children may forget what was underneath the Christmas tree—but may they never forget who was at the center of your home.
